lesson.title: Choosy by Design: How the Membrane Decides What Gets Through
lesson.summary: Selective permeability is the property that lets a cell's membrane act as both barrier and gate, freely admitting some molecules while requiring others to use dedicated protein transporters.
lesson.body:
Every property of the plasma membrane covered so far, its phospholipid bilayer, its fluid mosaic organization, its cholesterol, and its embedded proteins, comes together to produce one overarching functional trait: selective permeability. This means the membrane does not treat every molecule the same way. It allows some substances to cross freely, restricts others heavily, and actively controls a third group using specific transport proteins. That selectivity is what allows a eukaryotic cell to hold onto an internal chemical composition sharply different from its surroundings.

Which category a molecule falls into is determined mostly by its size, its polarity, and whether it carries an electric charge, properties that map directly onto the bilayer structure covered earlier. Small nonpolar molecules, such as oxygen, carbon dioxide, and nitrogen gas, dissolve readily into the hydrophobic interior of the phospholipid bilayer and diffuse straight through without any assistance. Small nonpolar steroid hormones behave the same way, which is part of why steroid hormone receptors are often found inside the cell rather than on its surface.

Water sits in an interesting middle category. It is small but polar, so it crosses the hydrophobic bilayer directly only slowly, yet cells frequently need to move large volumes of water quickly. The solution is a dedicated channel protein called an aquaporin, an integral membrane protein described in the previous chapter, that forms a narrow pore allowing water molecules through at a much faster rate than the bilayer alone permits, without letting ions or other solutes pass through the same channel.

Larger polar molecules, such as glucose and amino acids, and any charged ion, such as sodium, potassium, calcium, or chloride, cannot cross the hydrophobic bilayer directly at any meaningful rate, since the hydrophobic interior strongly repels anything charged or highly polar. These substances depend entirely on the transport proteins covered in the membrane proteins chapter, either channel proteins that form a selective pore or carrier proteins that bind the molecule and change shape to move it across. Without those specific proteins scattered through the membrane's fluid mosaic, glucose could sit right outside a cell that badly needs it and never get in.

This layered system, direct diffusion for a few small nonpolar substances, channel assistance for water, and dedicated transport proteins for everything else, is what gives the plasma membrane its selective character rather than making it either a solid wall or an open sieve. That selectivity sets up the two major transport categories covered in the chapters that follow: passive transport, where substances move down their existing gradient without requiring cellular energy, and active transport, where the cell spends energy to move substances against their gradient. Both depend entirely on the selective permeability established here.
